To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have identified four genomic regions significantly associated with straw lignin concentration in a barley population of 179 diverse accessions, and that these regions explained 22.5-38.7% (on average 31.5%) of the phenotypically observed variation.

we identified loci associated with the straw composition and energy value in barley and that we identified candidate genes for the lignin biosynthesis that are associated with the straw lignin content.

(i) barley straw is a promising feedstock for energy production, as its chemical composition is highly variable and can be modified by plant water status; (ii) lignin is an important trait that determines the energy value of straw; and (iii) genomewide association studies identified candidate loci that can be used in molecular breeding for the improvement of straw quality.

the development of a new generation of biofuels and bioenergy crops.

drought stress has an impact on the composition of the barley straw and the energy value.

we have identified a number of candidate genes for lignin content and composition that can be used in future breeding programs.

The main takeaway from our work is that

the genetic variation in straw quality is considerable, and the GWAS approach identified loci that could be associated to straw lignin content, a trait that has a strong effect on the energy value in both biological and thermochemical conversions.
the composition of the straw is crucial for the value of the straw as a source of biomass for bioenergy applications, and that the composition can be altered by drought and molecular breeding.

the genetic control of the composition of barley straw is complex, but it is possible to identify genomic regions that are associated with the composition of straw, as well as with the straw composition response to plant water status.
